title: Housing loans the City does not expect to collect
question: How much has the City lent for housing, how much of it does the City’s own financial report say will not be collected, and how much comes back each year?
finding: The City’s financial report for June 2025 says $3.16 billion of its $3.48 billion loan portfolio is not expected to be collected: 91%. Ten years earlier it was $1.00 billion of $1.08 billion (93%), so the portfolio has more than tripled while the share written down held steady. The report gives the reason: “Management has determined through policy that many of these loans may be forgiven or renegotiated and extended long into the future”. From fiscal 2019 to 2026 the ledger shows the housing offices lending $2.68 billion and taking back $176.9 million of principal and $73.5 million of interest: about 7 cents of principal for each dollar lent.
how: The portfolio and the amount not expected to be collected are one sentence of the loans-receivable note, read from each Annual Comprehensive Financial Report from fiscal 2015 to 2025. Loans out, principal repaid and loan interest are the ledger’s lines “Loans Issued By City” (with forgivable loans), “Loan Rev-Principal Repmt” and “Interest Earned - Loans-Leases” for the Mayor’s office accounts, which hold the housing office, and for the Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure. Repayments in a year are for loans made in earlier years, so the last column is a rough gauge, not a rate of repayment.
limits: These loans are designed this way, and the report says so. Affordable-housing loans are made, in the words of the same report’s bond note, as “non-performing long-term loans, with repayment from any project residual receipts”: repayment depends on a project having money left over. The report presents this as the design of the programme, not as losses: a loan not expected to be collected is not a loan gone bad, and the allowance is an accounting estimate, not a write-off of any named loan. The note covers housing and small-business loan programmes together, and a repayment in the ledger can be a payoff on refinancing as well as a payment from surplus. What would settle whether any given loan is performing as agreed: the housing office’s loan-by-loan ledger (borrower, balance, residual receipts received, last report filed), which is not published.
